title: the Shiva Purana (selections)
hook: the wedding procession arrives at the mountain king's palace, and the bride's mother, watching from the roof, sees the groom

segments.voice: Yesterday in the Shiva Purana, Parvati's tapas held, the mocking visitor turned out to be Shiva, and he agreed to marry her. Which effort did you keep going? Today, the wedding. Day one thousand one hundred twenty-two.

On the roof of the mountain king's palace, a mother is waiting to see her future son-in-law. Her name is Mena. Down the road comes the wedding procession, and it is splendid. Gods in bright clothes, on fine mounts, with music. Each time a shining figure goes by, Mena asks, is that him? Is that Shiva? And each time she's told, no, that's one of his guests. Then the rest of the procession comes around the bend. And the bride's mother, still on the roof, gets her first look at the groom.
screen: `A MOTHER ON THE ROOF.` → `IS THAT HIM? NO, A GUEST.` → `THEN THE GROOM COMES INTO VIEW.`

segments.voice: In the Shiva Purana's telling, Shiva's own companions, his ganas, come along behind the gods. Some have strange faces, some are like ghosts and goblins, some are howling and dancing. And in the middle of them rides Shiva on his bull, smeared with ash, snakes for ornaments, the clothes of a man who lives in cremation grounds. Mena faints. When she comes to, she's furious. She blames the sage Narada, who encouraged this match. She says she'd rather see her daughter dead than married to that. She will not give her away. Now listen to Parvati. She doesn't defend herself by pretending Shiva is ordinary. She simply says she will marry no one else. She has already chosen. The gods and sages plead with Mena. And then the story does something tender. Shiva, the god who burned Kama for trying to move him, bends for his mother-in-law. He takes on a form of great beauty, dressed and adorned like a bridegroom. Mena looks again, and this time she's delighted. The wedding goes ahead with music and rites, and the whole mountain celebrates. So who changed? Both of them, a little. Mena learns to look past the ash. Shiva lets the family see a face they can bear. Temple art remembers that second face. Images of Shiva as the handsome bridegroom, taking Parvati's hand, are called Kalyanasundara, the beautiful one of the wedding. And there's something homely inside it. Mena saw the ash first. Parvati saw who he was. A good wedding needs both: someone willing to look again, and someone willing to show a gentler side.
screen: `THE GROOM: ASH, SNAKES, A BULL.` · `MENA FAINTS AND SAYS NO.` · `PARVATI: NO ONE ELSE.` · `SHIVA SHOWS A GENTLER FACE.` · then, large: `LOOK AGAIN. SHOW A GENTLER SIDE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look again. Settle, and let the breath slow. Bring to mind someone whose ways are strange to you: a new in-law, a coworker, a neighbor whose life you don't understand. Notice what you see first, the way Mena saw the ash. Then ask quietly: what might someone who loves this person see? Stay there for a few breaths. Then turn it around. Is there someone who finds you hard to take? What gentler side of yourself could you let them see? If you pray, you can hold both people before Shiva, or before God, in your own words. The bell holds the time.
The Shiva Purana. Today's selection: the wedding, a mother who fainted at the groom, a bride who chose no one else, and a god who showed a gentler face.
Your line: the Shiva Purana, in selections. Today, give one person you've judged quickly a second look, and let one person see a softer side of you. Day one thousand one hundred twenty-two.

howItsDone: The wedding of Shiva and Parvati is retold in the Shiva Purana and other Puranas, and it is honored in temple festivals and in images of Shiva as Kalyanasundara, the bridegroom taking Parvati's hand.

fork.setup: you're Parvati. your mother has fainted at the sight of your groom and now refuses the match. what do you do?
options: agree to marry someone more suitable.
say you will marry no one else.
ask Shiva to stay away until she calms down.
fork.reveal: Parvati says plainly she has chosen and will marry no one else. then the gods plead, and Shiva himself shows a gentler face.

original.note: Sanskrit: Parvati, the daughter of the mountain, Shiva's bride in today's selection.

what it means: the bride sees who the groom is, the mother learns to look again, and the god shows a face she can bear.
what a scholar hears: Kalyanasundara, the beautiful one of the wedding, a form of Shiva shown in temple art taking Parvati's hand.

notes: Follows the 1121 writer's arc (pillar, Daksha, Kama, Parvati's tapas); this day is the wedding.

Confirm from the Shiva Purana, Rudra Samhita, Parvati Khanda: Mena watching from the palace roof and asking Narada 'is that Shiva?' as each god passes; the ganas' appearance; Mena fainting and blaming Narada; her saying she would rather her daughter die than marry him (paraphrased); Parvati refusing anyone else; Shiva taking a beautiful form so that Mena rejoices. Details of who persuades Shiva (Vishnu, Narada) vary by edition and were left out.
Kalyanasundara as the iconographic name of the wedding form; confirm gloss 'the beautiful one of the wedding'.
The garland of skulls is listed among Shiva's ornaments in the procession; confirm it appears in this passage or cut it.

Editor pass: cut the unconfirmed garland of skulls; changed 'the god who wouldn't budge for Kama's arrow' (1120 says the arrow did stir him) to 'the god who burned Kama for trying to move him'; replaced the generalization 'families meeting a newcomer often see the ash first' with the story's own pair, Mena and Parvati.
